cards.title: Constant-colour polynomial-time colouring of 3-colourable graphs
cards.formal: Do there exist an absolute integer \(C\geq3\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph promised to be \(3\)-colourable, outputs a proper colouring using at most \(C\) colours with probability at least \(2/3\)? The same palette bound and finite program must work for all graph sizes. This card retains the explicitly adopted randomized version of the constant-palette problem.
cards.definitions:
The input is an explicit finite simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), with \(n\geq1\), a unary size header and an adjacency matrix. There are no loops or parallel edges; isolated vertices count toward \(n\). The binary input length \(L\) is of order \(n^2+1\). The promise asserts the existence of a proper colouring with at most three colours, but supplies no colouring or other witness.

A proper \(k\)-colouring is a function \(c:[n]\to[k]\) with \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). A successful output explicitly lists one binary colour index in \([C]\) for each vertex, in vertex order. The algorithm may instead output a failure symbol. A candidate can be checked against the palette bound and all edges in polynomial time; invalid candidates can be converted to failure. Successful runs must colour every vertex and leave no monochromatic edge.

Use one randomized multitape Turing machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(K,d\) such that every computation takes at most \(K(L+1)^d\) bit operations on every graph and every random-bit sequence. All arithmetic precision, output and random-bit generation are included. The random bits are independent and fair, there are polynomially many of them in each run, and the machine has no advice or oracle. Deterministic algorithms are included. No correctness or success-probability requirement is imposed outside the three-colourability promise, but the time bound still applies.

For every promised graph, the probability of a valid \(C\)-colouring must be at least \(2/3\), over the internal bits alone. This is a guarantee for each individual input, not an average over random graphs. The existentially chosen \(C,K,d,A\) are fixed before the graph: \(C\) cannot depend on \(n\), degree, density or the particular input. The exponent and constants may depend on the selected palette bound because only one constant palette is required. Independent repetition can amplify the success probability after checking outputs; exact recognition of the three-colourability promise is not required.

There is no planarity, bounded-degree, expansion, forbidden-subgraph, random-input or supplied-decomposition assumption. A palette of six, one hundred or any other fixed integer could establish a positive answer. A number of colours growing with \(n\), however slowly, does not satisfy the constant-palette requirement.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of at least one such constant \(C\) and algorithm, or a proof in Lean that no such pair exists. A positive answer must verify all-input worst-case polynomial bit complexity and, for every promised graph, success probability at least \(2/3\) with a proper colouring of the full graph using that one palette.

A negative answer must exclude every absolute \(C\geq3\) and every uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm with the stated guarantee. Unconditional NP-hardness of each three-versus-\(C\) decision promise would give a complexity-theoretic obstruction, but deducing nonexistence of these randomized algorithms from it additionally requires \(\mathsf{NP}\ne\mathsf{RP}\). An unproved separation or Label Cover hypothesis cannot be treated as established in an answer to this unconditional question. Hardness for five colours alone, fixed-point-logic inexpressibility, an algorithm with a growing palette, partial colouring, or a restricted input family does not settle the full target.
cards.why: A defining promise-CSP problem: determine whether relaxing an NP-hard colouring task to any fixed larger palette permits efficient construction of a valid solution.

importance.reason: The paradigmatic approximate graph-colouring question, central to promise CSPs and to the gap between algorithmic relaxations and hardness with perfect completeness.

progress.text: Barto–Bulín–Krokhin–Opršal establish the NP-hardness of five-colouring three-colourable graphs; the full work appears in JACM in 2021.
Guruswami–Sandeep derive hardness for every fixed output palette from a d-to-1 conjecture with perfect completeness.
Kawarabayashi–Thorup–Yoneda obtain \(\widetilde O(n^{0.19747})\) colours using improved combinatorial progress combined with SDP methods.
Bansal–Huang–Lee improve the general polynomial-time upper bound to \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours through a new SDP-based analysis.
The revised Dawar–Molnár full version proves an all-constant obstruction for fixed-point logic with counting; it does not establish unrestricted computational hardness.

A new preprint claims NP-hardness for every fixed three-versus-k decision gap. Its full proof is not audited here, and even the asserted hardness alone would not unconditionally settle randomized algorithm existence.

context_blocks.text: The input comes with a guarantee that three colours suffice, but not with the partition into three independent sets. Allowing more colours is a relaxation of the output requirements. The question asks whether some fixed amount of this relaxation makes the problem efficiently solvable on every promised input. A mechanism for choosing 100 colours would qualify just as a mechanism for choosing six colours would; the constant need not be close to three.

This promise matters. Strong inapproximability results for the chromatic number on unrestricted graphs can use instances whose chromatic number grows with the graph size. They do not automatically establish hardness when the yes-instances must have chromatic number at most three. Conversely, an algorithm for planar graphs would use a structural assumption missing here. Three-colourable graphs can be dense and can have high-degree vertices.

The problem is a basic example of promise constraint satisfaction. An edge asks its two endpoints to receive different labels. The promise says the constraints have a solution over a three-element domain; the algorithm is allowed to use a larger fixed domain. In graph-homomorphism language, an input maps to \(K_{3}\) and the output must provide a map to \(K_{C}\). The associated decision promise distinguishes graphs mapping to \(K_{3}\) from graphs not mapping to \(K_{C}\).

The algebraic PCSP theorem gives unconditional NP-hardness of the three-versus-five decision gap. A randomized five-colouring search algorithm with the guarantee in this card would yield an RP algorithm for SAT after applying the reduction and checking its output, so excluding such a randomized algorithm requires \(\mathsf{NP}\ne\mathsf{RP}\). Here RP means polynomial time with no accepting computation on a NO-instance and acceptance probability at least one half on every YES-instance. The result addresses only small fixed palettes, leaving six, one hundred and every other larger constant unexcluded by that theorem alone.

A useful elementary observation is that the neighbours of any vertex in a three-colourable graph induce a bipartite graph: the vertex’s own colour cannot appear among its neighbours. Thus one can efficiently colour a large neighbourhood using two fresh colours. When all remaining degrees are small, greedy colouring is effective. Balancing these two procedures already gives an \(O(\sqrt{n})\)-colour algorithm. The challenge is to extract much more global information than this local observation provides.

Modern algorithms combine combinatorial reductions with semidefinite relaxations. The relaxation assigns vectors that mimic the separation of colours, and rounding extracts independent sets or other useful progress. Kawarabayashi, Thorup and Yoneda’s STOC 2024 work strengthens the combinatorial side and obtains \(\widetilde O(n^{0.19747})\) colours after combining it with the SDP approach. The suppressed factors are polylogarithmic in n.

Bansal, Huang and Lee’s February 2026 preprint improves the SDP analysis using third-level neighbourhoods and a new vector \(5/2\)-colouring construction. Combined with the combinatorial component, its theorem gives \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours. A vector \(5/2\)-colouring is a geometric relaxation, not an ordinary assignment using a fractional number of colours. The exponent improvement is real progress, while the final number of actual colours still grows with n.

Hardness evidence also goes beyond five colours under additional assumptions. Guruswami and Sandeep show that a fixed d-to-1 Label Cover conjecture implies hardness for every constant output palette. Their premise requires perfectly satisfiable yes-instances. Replacing perfect completeness by near-perfect completeness changes what the reduction guarantees, so established results about almost-satisfiable games cannot simply be substituted into this argument.

Dawar and Molnár’s full version, revised in March 2026, proves that fixed-point logic with counting cannot separate three-colourable graphs from graphs requiring more than any fixed number of colours. This is an unconditional obstruction for that logic on unordered structures, not for all polynomial-time algorithms on explicitly encoded graphs. The card sits at the intersection of approximation algorithms, algebraic reductions and limits of relaxation methods: a resolution would tell us how much a fixed expansion of the solution domain can help.

Fixed-point logic with counting augments first-order descriptions by iterative fixed points and counting operators. On unordered graphs it does not express every polynomial-time algorithm available on an explicit binary encoding. Thus the March 2026 theorem is an unconditional limitation of a powerful logic, but a different machine using the encoding’s order is not covered.

The14September2026 Fei–Minzer–Wang preprint claims a perfectly complete4-to-1 game theorem and, in Corollary1.7, NP-hardness of every fixed three-versus-k colouring gap. Its complete proof has not been independently audited here. If established, this removes the extra Label Cover conjecture from that hardness claim, but excluding the randomized search algorithms in this card would still require NP different from RP. The distinction follows because candidate colourings are efficiently checkable, giving one-sided error after a gap reduction.

cards.title: Hardness of 6-coloring 3-colorable graphs
cards.formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction \(R\) from Boolean \(3\)-SAT to finite simple undirected graphs such that, for every \(3\)-CNF formula \(F\),
\[
F\text{ is satisfiable}\ \Longrightarrow\ \chi(R(F))\leq3,
\qquad
F\text{ is unsatisfiable}\ \Longrightarrow\ \chi(R(F))>6?
\]
Equivalently, is the promise decision problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(K_3,K_6)\) NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? This is the previously approved gap-decision formulation of the six-colouring hardness question.
cards.definitions:
A Boolean \(3\)-CNF formula is a finite conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three literals. A literal is a Boolean variable or its negation. Variables and clause lists are explicitly encoded with binary indices and fixed delimiters; repeated literals and clauses are allowed. The empty conjunction is true and an empty clause is false. Let \(L\) be the complete encoding length.

The reduction is one deterministic multitape Turing machine. On every valid formula it outputs one graph \(G=R(F)\) on a labeled vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), allowing \(n=0\). Encode \(n\) by an explicit unary size header and then list unordered pairs of distinct binary vertex indices as edges, without repeated edges. Thus isolated vertices are included explicitly in the input size and the graph is not a succinct exponentially large object. There are fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that the entire computation, including writing the graph, takes at most \(C(L+1)^d\) bit operations. There are no random bits, advice or oracle calls. Malformed formulas may be rejected. The graph need not come with any colouring, satisfying assignment or other witness.

A proper \(k\)-colouring of a graph is a function \(c:[n]\to[k]\) such that \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). The chromatic number \(\chi(G)\) is the least such \(k\), with \(\chi\) of the empty graph defined as zero. For \(k\geq1\), \(K_k\) is the loopless complete graph on \([k]\). A graph homomorphism maps vertices to vertices and sends each edge to an edge, so a proper \(k\)-colouring is exactly a homomorphism to \(K_k\).

The promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(K_3,K_6)\) requires YES on graphs with \(\chi(G)\leq3\) and NO on graphs with \(\chi(G)>6\). Graphs of chromatic number four, five or six lie outside the promise; a decision algorithm may answer either way on them. The reduction itself must send every satisfiable formula to the YES region and every unsatisfiable formula to the NO region, so its valid outputs never lie in this middle region. It is a many-one reduction: it produces a single instance and does not query a colouring oracle.

The two reduction implications must hold without a Unique Games, Label Cover, or other unproved hypothesis. NP-hardness here denotes the existence of this unconditional reduction; it is not itself the assertion that the problem has no polynomial-time algorithm. Since Boolean \(3\)-SAT is NP-complete, the displayed reduction is equivalent to the standard deterministic many-one NP-hardness requirement for all NP languages.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a reduction exists, or a proof in Lean that no such reduction exists. A positive answer must specify the construction, prove its uniform polynomial bit complexity and verify both chromatic-number implications for every input formula. Hardness only under an unproved conjecture, a reduction with weaker completeness or soundness, or hardness for a different pair of palettes does not settle this target.

A negative answer must rule out all deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions satisfying the two implications. In particular, a polynomial-time algorithm for the promise problem alone does not unconditionally prove nonexistence of the reduction: combining both would imply \(\mathsf P=\mathsf{NP}\). If \(\mathsf P=\mathsf{NP}\), a SAT decider could itself construct such a reduction by returning \(K_3\) or \(K_7\) according to satisfiability. Failure of one algebraic gadget construction, inability to find a particular polymorphism, or a finite list of unsuccessful reductions is insufficient for the negative answer.
cards.why: The three-versus-six gap is a concrete fixed-template question in approximate colouring and promise constraint satisfaction. An established reduction would supply a fundamental obstruction to algorithms producing six-colour solutions on promised three-colourable inputs; the newly claimed all-constant result directly addresses this target.

importance.reason: A widely recognized frontier example for promise constraint satisfaction, explicitly posed beyond the known five-colour hardness. Kept separately from the all-constant algorithm question because it asks for an individually significant fixed-template reduction.

context_blocks.text: A promise of three-colourability guarantees that a small partition into independent sets exists but does not reveal it. Allowing six colours relaxes the requested output. The associated decision gap separates graphs admitting three colours from graphs that do not admit even six. This is a small fixed-template promise CSP with no growing palette parameter.

Barto, Bulín, Krokhin and Opršal prove hardness for distinguishing \(k\)-colourable graphs from graphs not colourable with \(2k-1\) colours, for every \(k\geq3\). At \(k=3\), the result gives a gap from three to five colours. Its NO-instances may still be six-colourable, so the theorem does not imply the three-versus-six gap.

The algebraic PCSP framework relates the available reductions to operations that preserve the promised constraint relations, called polymorphisms. The source demonstrates the strength of this approach with the five-colour theorem and explains that moving to larger palettes requires additional analysis. A limitation of one reduction family does not by itself show that the requested polynomial-time reduction cannot exist.

Bansal, Huang and Lee’s February 2026 theorem reports a polynomial-time algorithm using \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours on an \(n\)-vertex three-colourable graph. Their introduction still identifies five colours as the unconditional hardness frontier in its account. A growing-palette algorithm supplies neither a six-colouring algorithm nor a reduction proving hardness at six colours.

A deterministic polynomial-time six-colouring search algorithm on three-colourable inputs would yield a decision algorithm for this gap: run it with a polynomial time cutoff and check whether its output is a proper six-colouring. Every YES-instance would be accepted, while no NO-instance could pass the check. This one-way implication explains the relevance to search without identifying all possible notions of search hardness with the chosen decision reduction.

The separate question of whether some fixed constant palette allows polynomial-time colouring has a different quantifier. Hardness at six colours would not exclude an algorithm using seven, one hundred or another fixed number. Likewise, logarithmically many colours eventually exceed every fixed palette, so that algorithmic target is distinct from this hardness threshold.

The14September2026 preprint claims a perfectly complete4-to-1 game hardness theorem. Its Corollary1.7 explicitly gives the three-versus-k decision gap for every fixed k; taking k=6 would answer the present question affirmatively. This is an exact target match, not merely search hardness or an almost-satisfiable completeness statement. The full proof has not been independently verified in this review, so the result is recorded as a claimed resolution.

cards.context:
A promise of three-colourability guarantees that a small partition into independent sets exists but does not reveal it. Allowing six colours relaxes the requested output. The associated decision gap separates graphs admitting three colours from graphs that do not admit even six. This is a small fixed-template promise CSP with no growing palette parameter.

Barto, Bulín, Krokhin and Opršal prove hardness for distinguishing \(k\)-colourable graphs from graphs not colourable with \(2k-1\) colours, for every \(k\geq3\). At \(k=3\), the result gives a gap from three to five colours. Its NO-instances may still be six-colourable, so the theorem does not imply the three-versus-six gap.

The algebraic PCSP framework relates the available reductions to operations that preserve the promised constraint relations, called polymorphisms. The source demonstrates the strength of this approach with the five-colour theorem and explains that moving to larger palettes requires additional analysis. A limitation of one reduction family does not by itself show that the requested polynomial-time reduction cannot exist.

Bansal, Huang and Lee’s February 2026 theorem reports a polynomial-time algorithm using \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours on an \(n\)-vertex three-colourable graph. Their introduction still identifies five colours as the unconditional hardness frontier in its account. A growing-palette algorithm supplies neither a six-colouring algorithm nor a reduction proving hardness at six colours.

A deterministic polynomial-time six-colouring search algorithm on three-colourable inputs would yield a decision algorithm for this gap: run it with a polynomial time cutoff and check whether its output is a proper six-colouring. Every YES-instance would be accepted, while no NO-instance could pass the check. This one-way implication explains the relevance to search without identifying all possible notions of search hardness with the chosen decision reduction.

The separate question of whether some fixed constant palette allows polynomial-time colouring has a different quantifier. Hardness at six colours would not exclude an algorithm using seven, one hundred or another fixed number. Likewise, logarithmically many colours eventually exceed every fixed palette, so that algorithmic target is distinct from this hardness threshold.

The14September2026 preprint claims a perfectly complete4-to-1 game hardness theorem. Its Corollary1.7 explicitly gives the three-versus-k decision gap for every fixed k; taking k=6 would answer the present question affirmatively. This is an exact target match, not merely search hardness or an almost-satisfiable completeness statement. The full proof has not been independently verified in this review, so the result is recorded as a claimed resolution.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
